problems.title: Binary Pulsar
problems.statement:
Through systematic searches during the past decades, astronomers have found a large number of millisecond pulsars (spin period $< 10\ \mathrm{ms}$). Majority of these pulsars are found in binaries, with nearly circular orbits.

For a pulsar in a binary orbit, the measured pulsar spin period ($P$) and the measured line-of-sight acceleration ($a$) both vary systematically due to orbital motion. For circular orbits, this variation can be described mathematically in terms of orbital phase $\phi$ ($0 \le \phi \le 2\pi$) as,

$$P(\phi) = P_0 + P_{\mathrm{t}} \cos\phi \qquad \text{where } P_t = \frac{2\pi P_0 r}{c P_{\mathrm{B}}}$$

$$a(\phi) = -a_{\mathrm{t}} \sin\phi \qquad \text{where } a_{\mathrm{t}} = \frac{4\pi^2 r}{P_{\mathrm{B}}^2}$$

where $P_{\mathrm{B}}$ is the orbital period of the binary, $P_0$ is the intrinsic spin period of the pulsar and $r$ is the radius of the orbit.

The following table gives one such set of measurements of $P$ and $a$ at different heliocentric epochs, $T$, expressed in truncated Modified Julian Days (tMJD), i.e. number of days since MJD = 2,440,000.

| No. | T (tMJD) | P (μs) | a (m s$^{-2}$) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5740.654 | 7587.8889 | - 0.92 ± 0.08 |
| 2 | 5740.703 | 7587.8334 | - 0.24 ± 0.08 |
| 3 | 5746.100 | 7588.4100 | - 1.68 ± 0.04 |
| 4 | 5746.675 | 7588.5810 | + 1.67 ± 0.06 |
| 5 | 5981.811 | 7587.8836 | + 0.72 ± 0.06 |
| 6 | 5983.932 | 7587.8552 | - 0.44 ± 0.08 |
| 7 | 6005.893 | 7589.1029 | + 0.52 ± 0.08 |
| 8 | 6040.857 | 7589.1350 | + 0.00 ± 0.04 |
| 9 | 6335.904 | 7589.1358 | + 0.00 ± 0.02 |

By plotting $a(\phi)$ as a function of $P(\phi)$, we can obtain a parametric curve. As evident from the relations above, this curve in the period-acceleration plane is an ellipse.

In this problem, we estimate the intrinsic spin period, $P_0$, the orbital period, $P_{\mathrm{B}}$, and the orbital radius, $r$, by an analysis of this data set, assuming a circular orbit.

parts.label: (D1.1)
parts.statement: Plot the data, including error bars, in the period-acceleration plane (mark your graph as “D1.1”).

parts.label: (D1.2)
parts.statement: Draw an ellipse that appears to be a best fit to the data (on the same graph “D1.1”).

parts.label: (D1.3)
parts.statement: From the plot, estimate $P_0$, $P_{\mathrm{t}}$ and $a_{\mathrm{t}}$, including error margins.

parts.label: (D1.4)
parts.statement: Write expressions for $P_{\mathrm{B}}$ and $r$ in terms of $P_0$, $P_{\mathrm{t}}$, $a_{\mathrm{t}}$.

parts.label: (D1.5)
parts.statement: Calculate approximate value of $P_{\mathrm{B}}$ and $r$ based on your estimations made in (D1.3), including error margins.

parts.label: (D1.6)
parts.statement: Calculate orbital phase, $\phi$, corresponding to the epochs of the following five observations in the above table: data rows 1, 4, 6, 8, 9.

parts.label: (D1.7)
parts.statement: Refine the estimate of the orbital period, $P_{\mathrm{B}}$, using the results in part (D1.6) in the following way:

parts.label: (D1.7a)
parts.statement: First determine the initial epoch, $T_0$, which corresponds to the nearest epoch of zero orbital phase before the first observation.

parts.label: (D1.7b)
parts.statement:
The expected time, $T_{\mathrm{calc}}$, of the estimated orbital phase angle of each observation is given by,

$$T_{\mathrm{calc}} = T_0 + \left(n + \frac{\phi}{360^{\circ}}\right) P_{\mathrm{B}},$$

where $n$ is the number of full cycle of orbital phases that may have elapsed between $T_0$ and $T$ (or $T_{\mathrm{calc}}$). Estimate $n$ and $T_{\mathrm{calc}}$ for each of the five observations in part (D1.6). Note down difference $T_{\mathrm{O-C}}$ between observed $T$ and $T_{\mathrm{calc}}$. Enter these calculations in the table given in the Summary Answersheet.

parts.label: (D1.7c)
parts.statement: Plot $T_{\mathrm{O-C}}$ against $n$ (mark your graph as “D1.7”).

parts.label: (D1.7d)
parts.statement: Determine the refined values of the initial epoch, $T_{0,\mathrm{r}}$, and the orbital period, $P_{\mathrm{B,r}}$.

solution.statement:
**(D1.1)**

Graph Number : D1.1

- **Plot uses more than 50% of graph paper: 0.5**
- **Axes labels ($P$ and $a$): 0.5**
- **Dimensions of axes: 0.5**
- **Ticks and values on axes (or scale written explicitly): 0.5**
- **Points correctly plotted:**

| Points plotted | 9 | 8 | 7 | 6 | 5 | $< 5$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Marks given** | **4.0** | **3.5** | **3.0** | **2.0** | **1.0** | **0** |

**Correctness of points: deduction of 0.5 for each wrong point.**

- **Errorbars on points (at least 5): 1.0**

**(D1.2)**

See above

- **Elliptical curve with visual best fit: 1.0**
- **Curve symmetric about $a = 0$ line: 0.5**
- **Curve symmetric about some value of $P$ ($P \approx 7588.48$): 0.5**

**(D1.3)**

Values are determined from lengths of axes of ellipse and mid-point of $P$-axis.

Error margins may be determined by estimating extreme ellipses covering the points with errorbars. Any reasonable method of estimating error margins will be accepted.

$2P_{\mathrm{t}} = (1.34 \pm 0.04)\ \mathrm{\mu s}$ [$(13.4 \pm 0.4)\ \mathrm{cm}$ on graph]

$\boxed{P_{\mathrm{t}} = (0.67 \pm 0.02)\ \mathrm{\mu s}}$ **[2.0]**

$\boxed{P_0 = (7588.48 \pm 0.02)\ \mathrm{\mu s}}$ **[2.0]**

$2a_{\mathrm{t}} = (3.42 \pm 0.12)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ [$(17.1 \pm 0.6)\ \mathrm{cm}$ on graph] **[3.0]**

$\boxed{a_{\mathrm{t}} = (1.71 \pm 0.06)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}}$

- **Marking table:**

| Parameter | Half credit Minimum | Full credit Minimum | Full credit Maximum | Half credit Maximum |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $P_{\mathrm{t}}$(μs) | **0.59** | **0.63** | **0.71** | **0.75** |
| $\delta P_{\mathrm{t}}$(μs) | **0.01** | **0.02** | **0.04** | **0.05** |
| $P_0$(μs) | **7588.38** | **7588.43** | **7588.53** | **7588.58** |
| $\delta P_0$(μs) | **0.01** | **0.02** | **0.04** | **0.05** |
| $a_{\mathrm{t}}$(m s$^{-2}$) | **1.61** | **1.65** | **1.77** | **1.81** |
| $\delta a_{\mathrm{t}}$(m s$^{-2}$) | **0.04** | **0.05** | **0.07** | **0.08** |

- **Wrong values due to wrong/poor plot/fit in (D1.1) and (D1.2) WILL BE penalised.**
- **Error estimation is based on graph drawing. Quoted values correspond to the envelope of possible ellipses drawn to include all points with errorbars. Any reasonable method to estimate error to be given credit.**

**(D1.4)**

We can easily recover the orbital period ($P_{\mathrm{B}}$) and the radius of the orbit ($r$) in a circular orbit:

$$a_{\mathrm{t}} = \frac{4\pi^2}{P_{\mathrm{B}}^2} r$$

$$\therefore r = \frac{P_{\mathrm{B}}^2 a_{\mathrm{t}}}{4\pi^2}$$

**[1.0]**

$$P_{\mathrm{t}} = \frac{2\pi P_0}{P_{\mathrm{B}}} \times \frac{r}{c} = \frac{2\pi P_0}{P_{\mathrm{B}} c} \times \frac{P_{\mathrm{B}}^2 a_{\mathrm{t}}}{4\pi^2} = \frac{P_0 P_{\mathrm{B}} a_{\mathrm{t}}}{2\pi c}$$

$$\therefore \boxed{P_{\mathrm{B}} = \frac{P_{\mathrm{t}}}{P_0}\frac{2\pi c}{a_{\mathrm{t}}}}$$

**[1.0]**

$$r = \frac{a_{\mathrm{t}}}{4\pi^2}\left(\frac{P_{\mathrm{t}}}{P_0}\frac{2\pi c}{a_{\mathrm{t}}}\right)^2$$

**[1.0]**

$$\therefore \boxed{r = \left(\frac{P_{\mathrm{t}}}{P_0}\right)^2 \frac{c^2}{a_{\mathrm{t}}}}$$

**[1.0]**

**Alternative algebraic routes accepted. Each of $P_{\mathrm{B}}$ and $r$ carry 2.0 marks.**

**(D1.5)**

$$P_{\mathrm{B}} = \frac{P_{\mathrm{t}}}{P_0}\frac{2\pi c}{a_{\mathrm{t}}} = \frac{0.67}{7588.48} \times \frac{2\pi \times 2.998 \times 10^8}{1.71}\,\mathrm{s} = 96\,260\ \mathrm{s} = 1.125\,70\ \mathrm{d}$$

**[1.0]**

$$\Delta P_{\mathrm{B}} = P_{\mathrm{B}}\sqrt{\left(\frac{\Delta P_{\mathrm{t}}}{P_{\mathrm{t}}}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\Delta P_0}{P_0}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\Delta a_{\mathrm{t}}}{a_{\mathrm{t}}}\right)^2}$$

**[1.0]**

$$= 1.12570 \times \sqrt{\left(\frac{0.02}{0.67}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{0.02}{7588.48}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{0.06}{1.71}\right)^2}\,\mathrm{d} = 1.12570 \times 0.0461 \simeq 0.052\ \mathrm{d}$$

$$\therefore \boxed{P_{\mathrm{B}} = (1.13 \pm 0.05)\ \mathrm{d}}$$

**[1.0]**

$$r = \left(\frac{P_{\mathrm{t}}}{P_0}\right)^2 \frac{c^2}{a_{\mathrm{t}}} = \left(\frac{0.67}{7588.48}\right)^2 \times \frac{\left(2.998 \times 10^8\right)^2}{1.71}\,\mathrm{m}$$

$$\therefore r = 4.097\,39 \times 10^8\ \mathrm{m} = 2.738\,90 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{AU}$$

**[1.0]**

$$\Delta r = r\sqrt{\left(\frac{2\Delta P_{\mathrm{t}}}{P_{\mathrm{t}}}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{2\Delta P_0}{P_0}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\Delta a_{\mathrm{t}}}{a_{\mathrm{t}}}\right)^2}$$

**[1.0]**

$$= 2.738\,90 \times 10^{-3} \times \sqrt{\left(\frac{2 \times 0.02}{0.67}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{2 \times 0.02}{7588.48}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{0.06}{1.71}\right)^2}\,\mathrm{AU} = 2.738\,90 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.069\,25\ \mathrm{AU} \simeq 0.19 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{AU}$$

$$\boxed{r = (2.74 \pm 0.19) \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{AU}}$$

**[1.0]**

Errors in $P_{\mathrm{B}}$ and $r$ can be also estimated as maximum possible (worst case) error. In such case, errors would be about 1.5 times the standard error calculated above ($\delta P_{\mathrm{B}} = 0.07, \delta r = 0.25$).

**(D1.6)**

Using these newly determined orbital parameters, we can calculate the angular orbital phase for each data point, i.e., for each pair of acceleration and period measured ($P$, $a$).

$$\phi = \tan^{-1}\left(-\frac{a}{a_{\mathrm{t}}}\frac{P_{\mathrm{t}}}{P - P_0}\right)$$

Care has to be taken to choose the value of the phase from among $\phi, \pi \pm \phi, 2\pi - \phi$, depending on the sign of $\cos\phi$ and $\sin\phi$.

| Sr. no. | $T$ (tMJD) | $P$ (μs) | $a$ (m s$^{-2}$) | $\phi$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5740.654 | 7587.8889 | −0.92 | 148.62° |
| 4 | 5746.675 | 7588.5810 | +1.67 | 278.77° |
| 6 | 5983.932 | 7587.8552 | −0.44 | 164.57° |
| 8 | 6040.857 | 7589.1350 | +0.00 | 0.00° |
| 9 | 6335.904 | 7589.1358 | +0.00 | 0.00° |

- **Credit for each correct value: 1.0 for first three, 0.5 for last two.**
- **Credit for $\pi \pm \phi$ or $2\pi - \phi$ is 0.5 per value.**
- **All values wrong due to wrong expression for $\phi$ gets a maximum of 1.0 mark.**
- **Values in radians accepted.**

**(D1.7a)**

$$\frac{T_1 - T_0}{P_{\mathrm{B}}} = \frac{\phi_1}{2\pi} \Rightarrow T_0 = T_1 - \frac{\phi_1}{2\pi} P_{\mathrm{B}}$$

**[1.0]**

$$T_0 = 5740.654 - \frac{148.62^{\circ}}{360^{\circ}} \times 1.12570\ \mathrm{tMJD}$$

$$\boxed{T_0 = 5740.189\ \mathrm{tMJD}}$$

**[1.0]**

**Tolerance: $\pm 0.002$ tMJD. Using $P_0$ instead of $P_{\mathrm{B}}$ gets zero.**

**(D1.7b)**

$$T_{\mathrm{calc}} = T_0 + \left(n + \frac{\phi}{360^{\circ}}\right) P_{\mathrm{B}}$$

where $n =$ Integer part of $[(T - T_0)/P_{\mathrm{B}}]$.

| Sr. No. | $T$ (tMJD) | $\phi$ | $n$ | $T_{\mathrm{calc}}$ (MJD) | $T_{\mathrm{O-C}}$ (days) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5740.654 | 148.62° | 0 | 5740.654 | 0.000 |
| 4 | 5746.675 | 278.77° | 5 | 5746.689 | −0.014 |
| 6 | 5983.932 | 164.57° | 216 | 5983.855 | 0.077 |
| 8 | 6040.857 | 0.00° | 267 | 6040.751 | 0.106 |
| 9 | 6335.904 | 0.00° | 529 | 6335.684 | 0.220 |

**Deduction for each wrong/missing value of $n$, $T_{\mathrm{calc}}$ and $T_{\mathrm{O-C}}$: 0.5**

**No double penalty in one row.**

**(D1.7c)**

Graph Number : D1.7

- **Plot uses more than 50% of graph paper: 0.5**
- **Axes labels ($T_{\mathrm{O-C}}$ and $n$) including dimensions: 0.5**
- **Ticks and values on axes (or scale written explicitly): 0.5**
- **Points correctly plotted: 0.5 for each point**
- **Goodness of linear fit credited in next part**

**(D1.7d)**

A linear fit to the plot of $T_{\mathrm{O-C}}$ vs $n$ gives the offset of period per cycle (slope) and the shift in the zero-phase point (intercept). **[2.0]**

**This concept, which may be evident in the subsequent calculation, gains the credit, explicit statement is not necessary.**

From a linear fit,

Slope $= 0.000\,43\ \mathrm{d/n} \qquad$ Intercept $= -0.010\ \mathrm{d}$ **[3.0]**

- **Credit for good visual linear fit: 1.0**
- **Correct values of slope and intercept: 1.0 each**
- **Tolerance: $\pm 0.00002$ in slope and $\pm 0.002$ in intercept.**

$$T_{0,\mathrm{r}} = 5740.189 - 0.010 = \boxed{5740.179\ \mathrm{tMJD}}$$

**[1.0]**

$$P_{\mathrm{B,r}} = (1.12570 + 0.00043)\ \mathrm{d} = 1.126\,13\ \mathrm{d}$$

$$\boxed{P_{\mathrm{B}} = 1.1261\ \mathrm{d}}$$

**[1.0]**

**Incorrect sign of correction applied carries penalty of 0.5 for each quantity.**

Hand-drawn graph D1.7 on graph paper: T_O−C (days) from −0.05 to 0.25 against n from 0 to 540, five circled points and a straight-line fit; notes: x-axis 1 cm = 30, y-axis 1 cm = 0.02 days, origin (0,0), slope = 0.000426 day/cycle, intercept = −0.008 day.

Composite photograph of the Moon at seven times during the total lunar eclipse, arranged right to left and labelled 00:45, 01:40, 02:15, 02:47, 03:23, 04:00 and 04:50; the Earth’s shadow covers part of the disk in the 01:40 and 04:00 frames.
Diagram (not to scale) of the Earth with two rays S1R1 and S2R2 from opposite edges of the Sun crossing at the top of the Earth at angle θSun; a small circle labelled Moon on the left.

parts.label: (D2.1)
parts.statement:
In September 2015, apogee of the lunar orbit is closest to
New Moon / First Quarter / Full Moon / Third Quarter.
Tick the correct answer in the Summary Answersheet. No justification for your answer is necessary.

parts.label: (D2.2)
parts.statement:
In September 2015, the ascending node of lunar orbit with respect to the ecliptic is closest to
New Moon / First Quarter / Full Moon / Third Quarter.
Tick the correct answer in the Summary Answersheet. No justification for your answer is necessary.

parts.label: (D2.3)
parts.statement: Estimate the eccentricity, $e$, of the lunar orbit from the given data.

parts.label: (D2.4)
parts.statement: Estimate the angular size of the umbra, $\theta_{\mathrm{umbra}}$, in terms of the angular size of the Moon, $\theta_{\mathrm{Moon}}$. Show your working on the image given on the backside of the Summary Answersheet.

parts.label: (D2.5)
parts.statement:
The angle subtended by the Sun at Earth on the day of the lunar eclipse is known to be $\theta_{\mathrm{Sun}} = 1915.0''$. In the figure below, $S_1R_1$ and $S_2R_2$ are rays coming from diametrically opposite ends of the solar disk. The figure is not to scale.

Calculate the angular size of the penumbra, $\theta_{\mathrm{penumbra}}$, in terms of $\theta_{\mathrm{Moon}}$. Assume the observer to be at the centre of the Earth.

parts.label: (D2.6)
parts.statement: Let $\theta_{\mathrm{Earth}}$ be angular size of the Earth as seen from the centre of the Moon. Calculate the angular size of the Moon, $\theta_{\mathrm{Moon}}$, as would be seen from the centre of the Earth on the eclipse day in terms of $\theta_{\mathrm{Earth}}$.

parts.label: (D2.7)
parts.statement: Estimate the radius of the Moon, $R_{\mathrm{Moon}}$, in km from the results above.

parts.label: (D2.8)
parts.statement: Estimate the shortest distance, $r_{\mathrm{perigee}}$, and the farthest distance, $r_{\mathrm{apogee}}$, to the Moon.

parts.label: (D2.9)
parts.statement: Use appropriate data from September 10 to estimate the distance, $d_{\mathrm{Sun}}$, to the Sun from the Earth.

solution.statement:
**(D2.1)**

From the table we see that the angular size of Moon is smallest close to the New Moon day. Thus, the answer is $\boxed{\text{New Moon}}$. **[3.0]**

**Justification is NOT necessary for full credit.**

**(D2.2)**

As there is an eclipse happening in this month, the lunar nodes are close to Full Moon day and New Moon day. Next we notice that lowest declination of Moon is just 18°. This means that after the New Moon day, the orbit of Moon is above the ecliptic. In other words, the ascending node is near the $\boxed{\text{New Moon}}$. **[4.0]**

**Justification is NOT necessary for full credit.**

**(D2.3)**

The largest angular size of the Moon in the ephemerides is $2008.3''$ and the smallest angular size is $1763.7''$. The distance is inversely proportional to the angular size. Hence ratio of distance at perigee to the distance at apogee is:

$$\text{Ratio} = \frac{r_{\mathrm{perigee}}}{r_{\mathrm{apogee}}} = \frac{\cancel{a}}{1+e} \times \frac{1-e}{\cancel{a}}$$

**[2.0]**

$$\therefore \frac{1-e}{1+e} = \frac{1763.7}{2008.3} = 0.87821$$

$$\therefore e = \frac{1 - 0.87821}{1 + 0.87821} = 0.064846$$

$$\boxed{e \simeq 0.065}$$

**[2.0]**

**Rounding off is done to account for the fact that our data are not continuous, hence exact angular sizes at perigee and apogee are not known.**

**A non-rounded answer will also receive full credit.**

**(D2.4)**

The following construction is shown. **[5.0]**

Only two chords are necessary to determine the centre.

**The credit is divided in two parts for the drawing:**

- **Realisation that centre of umbra circle needs to be determined to find $\theta_{\mathrm{umbra}}$: 1.5**
- **Accurate determination of centre of umbra circle by geometric construction: 2.5**
  **Determination of centre of hand-drawn circle: maximum 1.5**
- **Measuring diameters of umbra and Moon: 0.5 each**

By estimating approximate centre of the shadow in the image, we find out,

$$\frac{\theta_{\mathrm{umbra}}}{\theta_{\mathrm{Moon}}} = \frac{d_{\mathrm{umbra}}}{d_{\mathrm{Moon}}} = \frac{9.1}{3.3} = 2.76$$

**[2.0]**

$$\therefore \boxed{\theta_{\mathrm{umbra}} \simeq 2.76\theta_{\mathrm{Moon}}}$$

**[1.0]**

**Acceptable range: $\pm 0.10$.**

**(D2.5)**

The following diagram needs to be drawn.

Angular size of umbra is $\theta_{\mathrm{umbra}} = 2\measuredangle BOQ$

Angular size of penumbra is $\theta_{\mathrm{penumbra}} = 2\measuredangle AOQ$

We have

$$\begin{aligned} QA &= QP + PA \\ &= OE + PE\tan\theta_1 \\ &\approx R_{\oplus} + d_{\mathrm{Moon}}\theta_1 && \text{since } PA \ll PE \\ &\approx R_{\oplus} + d_{\mathrm{Moon}}\frac{\theta_{\mathrm{Sun}}}{2} && \text{since } \theta_1 \approx \theta_2 \approx \theta_{\mathrm{Sun}}/2 \end{aligned}$$

**[2.0]**

and

$$\begin{aligned} QB &= QP - PB \\ &= OE - PE\tan\theta_2 \\ &\approx R_{\oplus} - d_{\mathrm{Moon}}\theta_2 \\ &\approx R_{\oplus} - d_{\mathrm{Moon}}\frac{\theta_{\mathrm{Sun}}}{2} \end{aligned}$$

**[2.0]**

$$\therefore \theta_{\mathrm{penumbra}} = 2\measuredangle AOQ = 2\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{QA}{OQ}\right) \approx 2\frac{QA}{OQ} \qquad \text{since } QA \ll OQ$$

$$= 2\frac{R_{\oplus} + d_{\mathrm{Moon}}\frac{\theta_{\mathrm{Sun}}}{2}}{d_{\mathrm{Moon}}} = \frac{2R_{\oplus}}{d_{\mathrm{Moon}}} + \theta_{\mathrm{Sun}}$$

**[1.0]**

and

$$\theta_{\mathrm{umbra}} = 2\measuredangle BOQ = 2\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{QB}{OQ}\right) \approx 2\frac{QB}{OQ}$$

$$= 2\frac{R_{\oplus} - d_{\mathrm{Moon}}\frac{\theta_{\mathrm{Sun}}}{2}}{d_{\mathrm{Moon}}} = \frac{2R_{\oplus}}{d_{\mathrm{Moon}}} - \theta_{\mathrm{Sun}}$$

**[1.0]**

Subtracting,

$$\theta_{\mathrm{penumbra}} - \theta_{\mathrm{umbra}} = 2\theta_{\mathrm{Sun}} \Rightarrow \theta_{\mathrm{penumbra}} = \theta_{\mathrm{umbra}} + 2\theta_{\mathrm{Sun}}$$

**[1.0]**

We have,

$$\theta_{\mathrm{umbra}} = 2.76\theta_{\mathrm{Moon}} \qquad \text{and } \theta_{\mathrm{Sun}} = 1915.0''$$

From the given data, $\theta_{\mathrm{Moon}} = 2008.3''$. **[1.0]**

Therefore,

$$\theta_{\mathrm{penumbra}} = 2.76\theta_{\mathrm{Moon}} + 2\frac{1915.0}{2008.3}\theta_{\mathrm{Moon}}$$

$$\boxed{\theta_{\mathrm{penumbra}} = 4.67\theta_{\mathrm{Moon}}}$$

**[1.0]**

**Acceptable range: $4.57\theta_{\mathrm{Moon}}$ to $4.77\theta_{\mathrm{Moon}}$.**

Alternative solution:

In the figure below, rays $HEA$ and $IFC$ are coming from one edge of solar disk and rays $HFD$ and $GEB$ are coming from the opposite edge. The observer ($O$) is assumed to be at the centre of the Earth. The Moon travels along the path $ABCD$ during the course of eclipse.

From figure,

$$\measuredangle AEB = \measuredangle GEH = \measuredangle HFI = \measuredangle DFC = \measuredangle EJF = \theta_{\mathrm{Sun}}$$

**[3.0]**

$$\theta_{\mathrm{umbra}} = \measuredangle BOC = 2.76\theta_{\mathrm{Moon}}$$

**[1.0]**

$$\theta_{\mathrm{penumbra}} = \measuredangle AOD$$

**[1.0]**

$$\measuredangle AOD = \measuredangle AOB + \measuredangle BOC + \measuredangle COD$$

$$\measuredangle AOB = \measuredangle AEB$$

**[1.0]**

$$\measuredangle COD = \measuredangle CFD$$

**[1.0]**

$$\theta_{\mathrm{penumbra}} \simeq \measuredangle AEB + \theta_{\mathrm{umbra}} + \measuredangle CFD = 2\theta_{\mathrm{Sun}} + 2.76\theta_{\mathrm{Moon}} = 2 \times 1915.0'' + 2.76 \times 2008.3''$$

$$\boxed{\theta_{\mathrm{penumbra}} = 9372.9'' = 4.67\theta_{\mathrm{Moon}}}$$

**[2.0]**

**(D2.6)**

From the Moon,

$$\theta_{\mathrm{Earth}} = \frac{2R_{\oplus}}{d_{\mathrm{Moon}}}$$

**[1.0]**

From part (D2.5),

$$\theta_{\mathrm{umbra}} + \theta_{\mathrm{penumbra}} = 2\theta_{\mathrm{Earth}}$$

**[2.0]**

$$\therefore \theta_{\mathrm{Earth}} = \frac{\theta_{\mathrm{umbra}} + \theta_{\mathrm{penumbra}}}{2} = \frac{2.76 + 4.67}{2}\theta_{\mathrm{Moon}} = 3.72\theta_{\mathrm{Moon}}$$

$$\boxed{\theta_{\mathrm{Moon}} = = 0.269\theta_{\mathrm{Earth}}}$$

**[2.0]**

Alternative solution:

Let us say that the Moon is at position of $B$. Thus, angular size of Earth as seen from this position will be, (see figure in the previous part)

$$\theta_{\mathrm{Earth}} = \measuredangle EBF = \measuredangle BFD$$

**[2.0]**

$$= \measuredangle BFC + \measuredangle CFD \simeq \theta_{\mathrm{umbra}} + \theta_{\mathrm{Sun}}$$

**[1.0]**

The angular size of the Full Moon on 28 September as seen in the table is $2008.3''$.

$$\theta_{\mathrm{Earth}} = 2.76 \times 2008.3'' + 1915.0'' = 7453.0''$$

$$\boxed{\theta_{\mathrm{Moon}} = 0.269\theta_{\mathrm{Earth}} = \frac{\theta_{\mathrm{Earth}}}{3.72}}$$

**[2.0]**

**(D2.7)**

Thus, the radius of Moon will be,

$$R_{\mathrm{Moon}} = \frac{R_{\oplus}}{3.72}$$

$$R_{\mathrm{Moon}} = \frac{6371}{3.72}$$

**[1.0]**

$$\boxed{R_{\mathrm{Moon}} \simeq 1713\ \mathrm{km}}$$

**[2.0]**

**Acceptable range: $\pm 20\ \mathrm{km}$.**

**(D2.8)**

The shortest and longest distances will be,

$$r_{\mathrm{perigee}} = \frac{2 \times 1713 \times 206265}{2008.3}$$

$$\boxed{r_{\mathrm{perigee}} = 3.52 \times 10^5\ \mathrm{km}}$$

**[2.0]**

$$r_{\mathrm{apogee}} = \frac{2 \times 1713 \times 206265}{1763.7}$$

$$\boxed{r_{\mathrm{apogee}} = 4.01 \times 10^5\ \mathrm{km}}$$

**[2.0]**

**(D2.9)**

On September 10, phase of Moon is 0.097 and elongation of Moon is 36.2°. Angular size of the Moon on this day is $1792.0''$. Therefore, distance to Moon (from Earth) on September 10 is

$$d_{\mathrm{Moon,10}} = \frac{2 \times 1713 \times 206265}{1792.0} = 3.94 \times 10^5\ \mathrm{km}$$

**[2.0]**

$$\text{Let } \measuredangle EMS = \phi_M, \quad \measuredangle ESM = \phi_S, \quad \measuredangle SEM = \phi_E$$

$$\therefore \phi_E = 36.2^{\circ}$$

**[1.0]**

$$\text{phase} = \frac{1 + \cos\phi_M}{2}$$

**[2.0]**

$$\therefore \phi_M = \cos^{-1}(2 \times \text{ phase } - 1) = \cos^{-1}(2 \times 0.097 - 1) = \cos^{-1}(-0.806) = 143.71^{\circ}$$

**[2.0]**

$$\phi_S = 180^{\circ} - \phi_E - \phi_M = 180^{\circ} - 36.2^{\circ} - 143.71^{\circ} = 0.09^{\circ}$$

**[1.0]**

Now using sine rule,

$$\frac{d_{\mathrm{Sun}}}{d_{\mathrm{Moon,10}}} = \frac{\sin\phi_M}{\sin\phi_S}$$

**[2.0]**

$$\therefore d_{\mathrm{Sun}} = \frac{3.94 \times 10^8 \times \sin 143.71^{\circ}}{\sin 0.09^{\circ}}$$

$$\boxed{d_{\mathrm{Sun}} = 1.48 \times 10^{11}\ \mathrm{m}}$$

**[1.0]**

problems.title: Type IA Supernovae
problems.statement:
Supernovae of type Ia are considered very important for the measurements of large extragalactic distances. The brightening and subsequent dimming of these explosions follow a characteristic light curve, which helps in identifying these as supernovae of type Ia.

Light curves of all type Ia supernovae can be fit to the same model light curve, when they are scaled appropriately. In order to achieve this, we first have to express the light curves in the reference frame of the host galaxy by taking care of the cosmological stretching/dilation of all observed time intervals, $\Delta t_{\mathrm{obs}}$, by a factor of $(1 + z)$. The time interval in the rest frame of the host galaxy is denoted by $\Delta t_{\mathrm{gal}}$.

The rest frame light curve of a supernova changes by two magnitudes compared to the peak in a time interval $\Delta t_0$ after the peak. If we further scale the time intervals by a factor of $s$ (i.e. $\Delta t_s = s\Delta t_{\mathrm{gal}}$) such that the scaled value of $\Delta t_0$ is the same for all supernovae, the light curves turn out to have the same shape. It also turns out that $s$ is related linearly to the absolute magnitude, $M_{\mathrm{peak}}$, at the peak luminosity for the supernova. That is, we can write

$$s = a + bM_{\mathrm{peak}}\ ,$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. Knowing the scaling factor, one can determine absolute magnitudes of supernovae at unknown distances from the above linear equation.

The table below contains data for three supernovae, including their distance moduli, $\mu$ (for the first two), their recession speed, $cz$, and their apparent magnitudes, $m_{\mathrm{obs}}$, at different times. The time $\Delta t_{\mathrm{obs}} \equiv t - t_{\mathrm{peak}}$ shows number of days from the date at which the respective supernova reached peak brightness. The observed magnitudes have already been corrected for interstellar as well as atmospheric extinction.

| **μ (mag)** | **34.27** | **35.64** | |
| **cz (km s$^{-1}$)** | **4515** | **9426** | **12060** |
| Δt$_{\mathrm{obs}}$ (days) | m$_{\mathrm{obs}}$ (mag) | m$_{\mathrm{obs}}$ (mag) | m$_{\mathrm{obs}}$ (mag) |
| -15.00 | 19.41 | 18.35 | 20.18 |
| -10.00 | 17.48 | 17.26 | 18.79 |

parts.label: (D3.1)
parts.statement: Compute $\Delta t_{\mathrm{gal}}$ values for all three supernovae, and fill them in the given blank boxes in the data tables on the BACK side of the Summary Answersheet. On a graph paper, plot the points and draw the three light curves in the rest frame (mark your graph as “D3.1”).

parts.label: (D3.2)
parts.statement: Take the scaling factor, $s_2$, for the supernova SN2006IS to be 1.00. Calculate the scaling factors, $s_1$ and $s_3$, for the other two supernovae SN2006TD and SN2005LZ, respectively, by calculating $\Delta t_0$ for them.

parts.label: (D3.3)
parts.statement: Compute the scaled time differences, $\Delta t_{\mathrm{s}}$, for all three supernovae. Write the values for $\Delta t_{\mathrm{s}}$ in the same data tables on the Summary Answersheet. On another graph paper, plot the points and draw the 3 light curves to verify that they now have an identical profile (mark your graph as “D3.3”).

parts.label: (D3.4)
parts.statement: Calculate the absolute magnitudes at peak brightness, $M_{\mathrm{peak,1}}$, for SN2006TD and $M_{\mathrm{peak,2}}$, for SN2006IS. Use these values to calculate $a$ and $b$.

parts.label: (D3.5)
parts.statement: Calculate the absolute magnitude at peak brightness, $M_{\mathrm{peak,3}}$, and distance modulus, $\mu_3$, for SN2005LZ.

parts.label: (D3.6)
parts.statement: Use the distance modulus $\mu_3$ to estimate the value of Hubble's constant, $H_0$. Further, estimate the characteristic age of the universe, $T_{\mathrm{H}}$.
